{
  "reframes": [
    {
      "bottleneck": "Cost is concentrated in the closed-loop stage: 150 rollouts x 135 features = 20,250 sequential 300-step episodes, each gated by a 150 ms VLA forward pass. This budget is spent uniformly on every feature, including the majority that do nothing, and rollouts are already independent so raw GPU count only buys the ~2x batching that RLinf-VLA demonstrated.",
      "assumption": "A feature's value can only be judged by closed-loop task success, so every candidate feature must pay the full 150-rollout price before anything is known about it.",
      "reframe": "Change the order of steps: screen all features open-loop first by steering and measuring divergence between steered and unsteered predicted actions on a fixed buffer of recorded observations, then pay closed-loop rollouts only for the top-k features by effect size. Compute then buys feature coverage instead of redundant rollouts.",
      "question": "On one LIBERO task with pi0.5, what is the Spearman rank correlation between per-feature open-loop steered-vs-unsteered action divergence (L2 on action tokens over a fixed observation buffer) and per-feature closed-loop success-rate delta across 10 features spanning the divergence range?",
      "measure": "Record ~200 unsteered episodes and their activations on one task (a few GPU-hours), apply each of the 135 steering vectors open-loop to get divergence scores (~1 A100-day, ~$25), then run 25 closed-loop rollouts for each of 10 chosen features in a batched simulator (~1 A100-day). Compute the rank correlation. No real robot needed.",
      "compute_after": "If the correlation holds, the same compute screens 10-100x more features per study, or the 135-feature sweep shrinks ~10x in cost, freeing budget to sweep features on contact-rich simulated tasks that currently get no coverage.",
      "exact": "Spearman rho between per-feature mean open-loop action divergence and per-feature closed-loop success delta, over 10 features, plus the recall of truly-effective features in the open-loop top-20.",
      "expected": "Rho >= 0.7 and top-20 recall >= 0.8 would make screening the default; even rho ~ 0.4 with a cheap top-20 cutoff cuts cost roughly 5x.",
      "fails_if": "Open-loop divergence does not predict closed-loop effect (compounding errors, features that only matter under contact and never fire on the recorded buffer), or all divergences are near zero so the ranking is noise.",
      "closest_prior": "The 420,000-rollout / 520-SAE sweep (arXiv 2603.19233) pays full closed-loop cost per feature; open-loop action-divergence is the standard cheap proxy in LLM activation-steering evals but is unpublished for VLAs."
    },
    {
      "bottleneck": "The binary success metric forces ~150 rollouts per condition to resolve an effect and yields one bit per episode; it also cannot ask whether steering controls any contact variable without a full validated cloth task, which simulation cannot currently provide.",
      "assumption": "The unit of evidence is task-level success on a rigid pick-and-place benchmark, so effects smaller than a success-rate swing, and any control of contact rather than motion, are invisible.",
      "reframe": "Change what is measured: replace binary success with a continuous physical readout (wrist force/torque trace, contact timing, peak grasp force) on a short instrumented real-robot task such as grasping a compliant object, and regress steering strength against the readout so each trial yields a slope. This tests control of contact behaviour directly and sidesteps the unvalidated cloth simulator.",
      "question": "On a real pi0.5-class arm grasping a deformable object with a wrist force/torque sensor, does any of ~10 candidate SAE or FFN steering directions produce a monotone change in peak grasp force (newtons) across 5 steering strengths, versus sham random directions?",
      "measure": "10 directions x 5 strengths x 5 repeats = 250 real grasps, roughly 1-2 robot-days (~$2-5k) plus trivial GPU time; fit slope per direction and compare against the null distribution from random directions. Cheapest kill-criterion: if even the strongest known steering feature shows no force-trace effect in 25 trials, stop.",
      "compute_after": "If slopes exist, a handful of real trials validates each candidate, so compute shifts to wide sim-screened sweeps with cheap real confirmation (~25 trials per candidate instead of 150), a ~30x reduction in the expensive stage; if no slope exists, the cloth/deformable steering question is dead regardless of compute.",
      "exact": "Slope in newtons per unit steering coefficient and its t-statistic per direction, against the null distribution from random directions, plus minimum detectable effect at 25 trials.",
      "expected": "Given Grant et al. found motor programs bound to absolute coordinates (50/50 grasps at the recorded spot), at least one direction should shift applied force or contact timing measurably within 25 trials.",
      "fails_if": "No direction moves the force trace beyond trial-to-trial noise, meaning steering modulates high-level plans but not contact execution, so no sweep size can reveal cloth control that is not there.",
      "closest_prior": "Grant et al. motor-program binding on UR10e; COAST conceptors reporting +40% on three real tasks with binary metrics only; Goodfire marketing steering for robotics with no published numbers."
    },
    {
      "bottleneck": "For cloth and dish-rack tasks the binding constraint is not throughput but validity: steering effects measured in simulation are asserted not to transfer for deformables, so every additional simulated rollout buys more of the same rigid-task evidence and nothing about the actual blocker.",
      "assumption": "The answer needed is 'which features control cloth behaviour', which presumes a trustworthy cloth simulator; without one, sim compute is uninformative and the sim-vs-real transfer of steering effects has never been measured even where it could be.",
      "reframe": "Change the objective: before sweeping anything new, calibrate the sim-to-real transfer function of steering effect sizes on rigid tasks where both sides are cheap. If per-intervention effect direction and magnitude correlate between a GPU-parallel simulator and the real robot, simulation becomes a validated screening instrument; independently, measure whether the simulator predicts force traces for compliant objects, which is the fidelity threshold cloth screening would require.",
      "question": "Across >= 10 steering interventions on rigid DROID-style tasks, what is the sign agreement and rank correlation between each intervention's success-rate delta in a batched simulator (200 rollouts) and on the real robot (25 trials)?",
      "measure": "10 interventions x 200 batched sim rollouts (~1 A100-day, ~$25) + 10 x 25 real trials (~1-2 robot-days, ~$2-5k). Report sign agreement and Spearman rho of the deltas. Separately, log sim-vs-real wrist force traces on one compliant grasp and report trace error.",
      "compute_after": "If sign agreement >= 9/10 and rho >= 0.8, every GPU-dollar afterward buys validated screening and the field can cheaply sweep deformable-adjacent proxies; if agreement is poor, all sim spending on steering should stop and compute should be redirected to real-robot parallelization (many arms, many objects) instead.",
      "exact": "Sign-agreement rate and Spearman rho of per-intervention sim vs real success deltas, plus sim-vs-real force-trace RMSE on the compliant-grasp probe.",
      "expected": "Rigid-task transfer plausibly holds (consistent with sim benchmarks and RLinf-VLA throughput results) but is unmeasured for steering; the force-trace probe on a compliant object is expected to show a clear gap, quantifying exactly how far sim is from supporting cloth claims.",
      "fails_if": "Even 2-3 of 10 rigid interventions flip sign between sim and real, showing sim sweeps are noise for steering specifically, in which case more GPU compute only buys faster wrong answers.",
      "closest_prior": "RLinf-VLA (1.61-1.88x with 256 ManiSkill environments) establishes the throughput side but not effect transfer; no published sim-vs-real correlation of steering effect sizes exists; the 420k-rollout sweep (arXiv 2603.19233) is entirely rigid-task and does not test transfer."
    }
  ]
}
